title: The Coca-Cola Company
wiki_lead:
The Coca-Cola Company is an American multinational corporation founded in January 1892, headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia. It manufactures, sells and markets soft drinks including Coca-Cola, other non-alcoholic beverage concentrates and syrups, and alcoholic beverages. Its stock is listed on the New York Stock Exchange and is a component of the DJIA and the S&P 500 and S&P 100 indices. 
Coca-Cola was developed in May 1886 by pharmacist John Stith Pemberton. At the time it was introduced, the product contained the stimulants cocaine from coca leaves and caffeine from kola nuts, which together acted synergistically. The coca and the kola are the source of the product name and led to Coca-Cola's promotion as a "healthy tonic". In 1889, the formula and brand were sold for $2,300 (equivalent to $75,000 in 2025) to Asa Griggs Candler, who incorporated the Coca-Cola Company in Atlanta in 1892. The company has operated a franchised distribution system since 1889.  The global corporation has grown to market and sell over 500 drinks and brands across 200 countries by 2020.
The company largely produces syrup concentrate, which is then sold to various bottlers throughout the world who hold exclusive territories. The company is well known for its marketing and sponsorship programs, being a major sponsor in Global sporting events like the FIFA World Cup. The large scale of the country, and wide distribution, has also drawn criticism, including for failing to address sustainability and the health impacts of their products. Each year Coca-Cola brands produce 3 million tonnes of plastic packaging, including 110 billion plastic bottles. A 2024 study found that over 11% of branded plastic materials found as plastic pollution came from Coca Cola.

History

In July 1886, pharmacist John Stith Pemberton from Columbus, Georgia, invented the original Coca-Cola drink, which was advertised as helpful in the relief of headaches and to be placed on sale primarily in drugstores as a medicinal beverage. Pemberton had made many mixing experiments and reached his goal during the month of May, but the new product was as yet unnamed and uncarbonated. Pemberton's bookkeeper, Frank Mason Robinson, is credited with naming the product and creating its logo. Robinson chose the name Coca-Cola because of its two main ingredients (coca leaves and kola nuts) and because it is an alliteration. John Pemberton had taken a break and left Robinson to make, promote, and sell Coca-Cola on his own. Robinson promoted the drink with the limited budget that he had and succeeded.
American businessman Asa Griggs Candler purchased the Coca-Cola formula and brand, forming the Coca-Cola Company in Atlanta in 1892. By 1895, Coca-Cola was being sold nationwide. In 1919, the company was sold to Ernest Woodruff's Trust Company of Georgia, after which it was soon reincorporated under the Delaware General Corporation Law that same year.

grok_lead: The Coca-Cola Company is an American multinational corporation founded on May 8, 1886, by Atlanta pharmacist John Stith Pemberton as a syrup-based tonic sold at Jacobs' Pharmacy, initially containing coca leaf extract (including cocaine until its removal in 1903) and kola nut for caffeine. Incorporated in 1892 and headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia, it operates as a total beverage company, manufacturing and marketing concentrates and syrups for over 200 brands of non-alcoholic drinks, including its flagship Coca-Cola, distributed through independent bottling partners in more than 200 countries and territories, with daily consumption exceeding 2.2 billion servings. As of February 11, 2026, the company, listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker KO, generates trailing twelve-month revenues of approximately $47 billion and maintains a market capitalization of approximately $351 billion. The company's growth stems from aggressive franchised bottling, innovative marketingâsuch as pioneering contour bottle design in 1915 and associating the brand with cultural iconsâand expansion into diverse categories like waters, juices, and low/no-sugar variants amid shifting consumer preferences. Employing over 700,000 people through its system, Coca-Cola has achieved enduring global dominance in sparkling beverages, yet faces empirical scrutiny for contributing to obesity and diabetes through high-sugar formulations, with meta-analyses linking regular sugary drink intake to weight gain independent of total energy intake. Notable controversies include documented water depletion and contamination allegations in regions like India, where operations have been tied to groundwater overuse, and environmental critiques over plastic packaging, as the company produces billions of single-use bottles annually despite recycling initiatives. Additionally, revelations of corporate influence on public health research, such as funding the Global Energy Balance Network to emphasize physical activity over dietary factors in obesity, highlight tensions between commercial interests and causal evidence favoring reduced sugar consumption. These issues underscore ongoing debates about the beverage industry's role in public health and sustainability, balanced against its economic scale and innovation in reducing sugar content in response to regulatory pressures.
